newsitem.title: USA: Sounding desperate, Dole lashes out.
newsitem.headline: Sounding desperate, Dole lashes out.

text.p: An angry and frustrated Bob Dole on Thursday lashed out at voters, the media and the White House and appealed to America to wake up before it was too late to stop President Bill Clinton being re-elected.

His last-minute effort to persuade Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to drop out of the presidential race apparently a failure, Dole resumed the drive for votes in Florida -- a traditionally Republican state now leaning towards Clinton.

The Republican presidential nominee made no reference to Perot at a rally at a junior college here, but sounded angry and frustrated as he slashed away at Clinton's ethics and warned voters to wake up before it was too late.
"This is a very important election. And I know everybody gets frustrated. I even get frustrated and I'm the most optimistic man in America," Dole said.
"I wonder sometimes what people are thinking about or if people are thinking at all if they've really watched this administration, watched what's happening in the White House," he said.

Dole directed much of his ire at what he termed the liberal media, slammed the White House for taking campaign contributions from a convicted drug dealer and warned that Clinton had tarnished America's reputation in the world.

"We know the liberal media's not going to report on all these things because they want him re-elected ... But the country does not belong to the liberal media, nor does it belong to Bill Clinton. It belongs to the people of the United States," Dole said.
"We need to wake America up. It's (Election Day) 12 days away. Wake up America, you're about to do yourselves an injustice if you vote for Bill Clinton," he said.

Reflecting the campaign's desperation for a breakthrough to change the tide, Dole campaign manager Scott Reed was sent to Dallas on Wednesday to try to persuade the Texas billionaire to drop his independent campaign for the presidency.
Dole refused to answer reporters' repeated questions about Perot. As he left his hotel for the morning rally, Dole quipped "If you see Ross Perot tell me."
Perot won 19 percent of the vote in the 1992 presidential election. Many voters have deserted his candidacy this time around and he has only about 4-8 percent public support in recent polls.

It is unclear why Dole thought Perot would be open to his request. Relations between the two campaigns have not been cordial, with Dole supporting Perot's exclusion from the recent presidential debates. Perot has also been running ads criticising both Clinton and Dole on campaign finance reform.
Still, the Dole campaign hoped if Perot dropped out some of his supporters might move their way, making a difference in close states.
From Florida, Dole travels to Alabama, Louisiana and Texas on Thursday, trying to shore up his base in the South -- normally a Republican stronghold.

But Dole and Clinton are running dead even in Florida, which has not voted for a Democrat since Jimmy Carter in 1976. The race is also tight in Texas -- another state that has not seen a Democratic victory for 20 years.
The Dole campaign plans to target millions of dollars in California in the closing days, but a Los Angeles Times polls showed Dole lagging Clinton by 20 points in that state.
